list.listitem: Evaluate for secondary causes of eosinophilic pneumonia (EP) once an initial diagnosis is made. C
Idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia (IAEP) presents as acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); peripheral eosinophilia may not appear for several days. C
Idiopathic eosinophilic pneumonia with extrapulmonary symptoms suggests Churg-Strauss syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis, or hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES). C
Treat both IAEP and idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (ICEP) with high-dose corticosteroids. C

Expect a full recovery with properly treated IAEP, but ICEP will frequently relapse and requires corticosteroids for six months with a slow taper. B Case studies support use of monoclonal antibodies, particularly targeting IL-5 (mepolizumab and reslizumab) and IL-5R (benralizumab), in cases of ICEP resistant or intolerant to corticosteroids. C

background.definition: Eosinophilic pneumonia (EP) is prominent infiltration of the lung parenchyma by eosinophils.

list.listitem: Rare: there have been less than 400 cases reported in the literature of idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia (IAEP).

A 2004 investigation among 183,000 military personnel stationed in or near Iraq identified 18 cases of acute EP (AEP) for an incidence of 9.1 per 100,000 person-years; many were believed to be smoking-related.

Using a national inpatient database in Japan over approximately 5 years, authors identified 213 inpatients with AEP with a bimodal peak age distribution – 15-24 years, with cases clustered in summer months among those <40 years, and 65-79 years.
Incidence of idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (ICEP) is unknown, but appears to be higher than IAEP.
Primary or idiopathic causes have no known etiology.

Secondary causes are many and include drugs (hypersensitivity reaction), infections (parasitic, fungal, viral [influenza A H1N1, COVID-19], tuberculosis), malignancy, and systemic disease (postradiation pneumonitis, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, Sjögren’s). Drugs implicated include the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g., mesalamine, naproxen, ibuprofen), chemotherapeutic agent lenalidomide, antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, daptomycin, vancomycin, imipenem/cilastatin), amiodarone, antipsychotics risperidone and clozapine, anticonvulsants levetiracetam and gabapentin, and monoclonal antibodies (e.g., nivolumab, trastuzumab, and ustekinumab).There have also been two reports of AEP following pneumococcal and m-RNA COVID-19 vaccination.
A review of 196 case reports found that daptomycin was the most common cause of drug-induced eosinophilic pneumonia
Cigarette and marijuana smoking as well as second-hand smoke and vaping have all been implicated as triggers for AEP, especially among those reporting a recent change in smoking habits.

Loffler's syndrome (simple eosinophilic pneumonia) is a classic cause of EP associated with transient interstitial infiltrates and eosinophilia. The disease is usually mild and frequently associated with drugs or larval migration into the lungs in individuals with parasitic (helminthic) infections.
In a case series of 36 patients with AEP from a single institution over 18 years, 19 were idiopathic, 11 were smoking-related, and 6 were medication-related.
In a case series of 687 patients with eosinophilic pleural effusions, the most common causes were malignancy (26%) and pneumonia (13%); one quarter were deemed idiopathic.

The physiologic role of the eosinophil remains unclear. It is thought that the release of toxic substances by activated eosinophils in tissues may contribute to the pathophysiology of eosinophilic disorders.

In AEP, airway epithelial injury, endothelial injury, and release of interleukin (IL)-33 appear to recruit eosinophils to the lung which results in eosinophilic infiltration, degranulation and subsequent lung inflammation.

IL-5 may play a key role in idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (ICEP) and accumulation of eosinophils in the lungs. Recently, investigators found that purified human eosinophils stimulated with IL-5 predominantly secreted CCL4 which appears to act as a chemoattractant for eosinophils. Other chemokines that may play a role in accumulation or activation of eosinophils in EP are CCR3/CCR5 ligands along with lipid mediators and extracellular matrix proteins, all increased in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid from patients with EP.

In one study of patients with AEP, CEP, and agiitis-related EP, the levels of IL-33 and tryptase, a secretory granule-derived serine proteinase contained in mast cells and used as a marker for mast cell activation, were higher in recurrent cases compared to cases with nonrecurrent CEP.
Suspect eosinophilic pneumonia in patients with pulmonary infiltrates and evidence of peripheral eosinophilia and/or >25% eosinophils on examination of bronchioalveolar (BAL) fluid. C
Secondary causes of pulmonary eosinophilia (e.g., drugs, parasitic infections, autoimmune disease) should be ruled out. C
If there are extrapulmonary symptoms, including end-organ damage, consider Churg-Strauss syndrome, Wegener's granulomatosis, or hypereosinophilic syndrome. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Systemic involvement, nephropathy, neuropathy, skin lesions; P-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), Myeloperoxidase antibodies
End-organ damage, may involve the heart, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, kidney, or liver; lung is involved in one quarter of patients

Differential.Differential_Name: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
Differential.Differential_Features: Fever, rash, internal organ involvement, medication commonly associated with eosinophilic pneumonia
Travel to endemic area, GI symptoms
History of asthma, IgE antibodies to Aspergillus, Serum IgE >1000 ng/mL, evidence of bronchiectasis
Less than 25% eosinophils in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, no peripheral eosinophilia

Differential.Differential_Name: Autoimmune disease (Sjögren’s syndrome, systemic Lupus erythematosus, ulcerative colitis)

Differential.Differential_Features: Extrapulmonary involvement, lymphadenopathy, continued symptoms after corticosteroid treatment
No peripheral eosinophilia, unilateral consolidation of the lung, response to antibiotics

Differential.Differential_Name: Acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome
Differential.Differential_Features: Evidence of end-organ damage or severe extrapulmonary involvement, distinguish from IAEP by <25% eosinophils on BAL fluid
Systemic signs and symptoms, especially nephropathy, C-ANCA, Proteinase 3 antibodies

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: The modified Philit criteria, often used to diagnose AEP in research studies, are: 1) acute febrile illness of less than or equal to 1 month duration, 2) pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiography or computed tomography (CT), 3) pulmonary eosinophilia demonstrated by >25% eosinophils in BAL fluid OR eosinophilic pneumonia on lung biopsy (bronchoscopic or surgical), and 4) absence of other specific pulmonary eosinophilic diseases including eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), hypereosinophilic syndrome, and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

list.listitem: IAEP may present with acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). The presenting symptoms consist of the acute onset of high fever (77-100%), dyspnea (82-100%), cough (67-82%), and chest pain (16-56%). Up to 80% have crackles on chest auscultation.
Generally, IAEP has an acute onset, with symptoms having appeared for a few days. The average patient is between the ages of 25 and 30 years, but IAEP may present at any age.
IAEP appears to be associated with environmental respiratory exposures as well as recent initiation of tobacco smoking or increased frequency of smoking.

ICEP is more indolent than IAEP. The presenting symptoms consist of cough (60-94%), weakness (88.3%) fever (77.4%), weight loss (75%), and dyspnea (20-50%). Night sweats, fever, wheezing, sputum or loss of appetite/weight can also be present, while chest pain seems rare. Most patients do not develop acute respiratory failure and acute hypoxemia.
The duration of symptoms is usually greater than one month.
The most common age of presentation for ICEP is between 30 and 50 years. There is a 2.1:1 female:male predominance.

Extrapulmonary findings such as rash, renal failure, cardiac disease, hepatitis, or any other end-organ damage suggests an alternative diagnosis such as HES, Churg-Strauss syndrome, or a secondary cause of eosinophilic pneumonia (see ).

Initial diagnostic tests should include a chest x-ray (CXR) and complete blood count. Occasionally, findings may not be apparent on CXR but appear on chest computed tomography (CT). Evidence of bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates by either CXR or chest CT are necessary for diagnosis.,
Other CXR findings of eosinophilic lung disease include consolidation, ground-glass opacities, nodules, and masses.

CT findings of diffuse ground-glass attenuation and traction bronchiectasis were associated with death from AEP in a Japanese case series; traction bronchiectasis was present in 6 patients, 4 of whom died, but in none of the patients with smoking-related AEP, all of whom survived.

In an attempt to find a diagnostic method that would avoid bronchoscopy, authors of a retrospective study of 414 male military patients with pneumonia found 10 clinical and imaging variables via LASSO regression that could differentiate between AEP and other forms of pneumonia. These were: new-onset or recently increased smoking (≤4 weeks) (8 points), interlobular septal thickening (5 points), absence of sputum (3 points), ground glass opacity (3 points), acute onset (≤3 days) (2 points), dyspnea (2 points), chest pain (2 points), leukocytosis (2 points), bronchovascular bundle thickening (2 points), and bilateral involvement (2 points). Using a cut-off value of ≥18, 96.3% of patients could be correctly classified with a sensitivity of 94.44%, specificity of 96.58% and area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve of 0.997 (95% CI, 0.992 to 1.000) in the derivation group and 0.985 (95% CI, 0.965 to 1.000) in the validation group. AEP was diagnosed using the modified Philit criteria and was identified in 54 of 279 patients (19.4%) in the derivation group and 18 of 135 patients (13.3%) in the validation group.

A complete blood count showing eosinophilia and/or a BAL with >25% eosinophils is also necessary for diagnosis. Eosinophilia is defined as an absolute eosinophil count of greater than 500 cells per mm3. Most patients will have counts greater than 1500 eosinophils per mm3 and some greater than 5000 eosinophils per mm3. Important exceptions include IAEP, where peripheral eosinophilia may not manifest until three days after presentation.

To exclude known secondary causes, stool, sputum, and BAL fluid can be examined for ova and parasites if the patient has traveled to an endemic area. ELISA to toxocara canis can be done if the patient's history is consistent with exposure.
If allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is considered, perform serum IgE level, antibodies to aspergillus, and look for central bronchiectasis on CT of the chest.
If additional infections are considered, a purified protein derivative (PPD) should be placed and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test should be performed as well as blood and urine cultures.

If autoimmune disease and/or vasculitis are considered, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), anti-nuclear antibody (ANA), and rheumatoid factor should be performed. Definitive diagnosis for these entities may require tissue biopsy.
If malignancy is likely, tissue biopsy (if not contraindicated) of the involved organ(s) is suggested.

For suspected primary eosinophilia, a review of blood and marrow is suggested with standard cytogenetics, fluorescent in situ-hybridization, flow immunocytometry, and T-cell clonality and assessment to detect histopathologic or clonal evidence for an acute or chronic myeloid or lymphoproliferative disorder.

In one Korean study, the pretreatment fraction of exhaled nitric oxide was significantly higher in patients with AEP than in those without AEP (48 parts per billion [ppb] [range, 10-138] vs 14 ppb [range, 5-41]). A cut-off value of 23.5 ppb predicted AEP with a sensitivity of 0.87 and a specificity of 0.83. Post-treatment fraction of exhaled nitric oxide was similar between groups.
The diagnosis of eosinophilic pneumonia requires (1) pulmonary infiltrates on CXR or chest CT and (2) evidence of peripheral eosinophilia and/or >25% eosinophils on examination of BAL fluid.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with eosinophilic pneumonia.
For IAEP with significant hypoxemia, high-dose IV corticosteroids are recommended. Switch to oral corticosteroids once the patient can safely tolerate oral medications and treat for 2 to 4 weeks. B
For ICEP, high-dose oral corticosteroids are also recommended at 1 mg/kg prednisone for 6 months, with a slow taper to prevent relapse. B
Biologic therapies can be considered for relapsing ICEP, based on limited data. C

IAEP: High-dose corticosteroids are recommended such as IV methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg every 6 hours for patients with severe hypoxemia. Once the patient has shown improvement and can safely take oral medications, he or she can be treated with oral prednisone. Corticosteroids should be tapered over 2 to 4 weeks. A retrospective cohort study found no eifference in outcomes between 2 and 4 weeks of corticosteroids.

ICEP: High-dose oral corticosteroid therapy. Average dose studied was 1 mg/kg of oral prednisone. 82% of patients show subjective improvement within 48 hours of initiating corticosteroids. Because of the frequency of relapses, it is recommended to continue corticosteroid treatment and taper slowly over six months.

The US Food and Drug Administration approved use of eosinophil-specific biologic therapies targeting IL-5 (mepolizumab and reslizumab) and IL-5R (benralizumab) based on supportive data for treating eosinophilic asthma, HES, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis. Detailed information on biologic treatments for these disorders, as well as eosinophilic pneumonia, can be found in the cited review.

In a case report of a patient with ICEP who required prolonged steroids causing side effects, omalizumab was found helpful as a steroid-sparing adjunct. Several other case reports also found single-dose benralizumab effective in resolution of ICEP.

In a case series of 10 patients with ICEP and a median follow-up of 9 months, mepolizumab, a humanized antibody directed against IL-5, was successful in remission of lung lesions and reducing disease exacerbations and corticosteroid use. Complete resolution of ICEP for 2 years was also reported with use of mepolizumab in a case of a 55-year-old woman with comorbid cough-variant asthma, and the drug was successful in treating a severe case of DRESS with pulmonary failure. Monthly subcutaneous mepolizumab was successful in another care report of ICEP poorly responsive to steroids.

In another case series of 30 patients with ICEP, 12 patients (40.0%) recurred after corticosteroid dose tapering. Nine of these patients were treated with maintenance doses of corticosteroid. Of ICEP patients who experienced recurrence, 6 had relapses 2 or more times and 4 patients were successfully treated with anti-IL-5 agents; in 3 patients, corticosteroids were withdrawn.

Follow standard guidelines for antibiotics in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). While macrolides and respiratory fluoroquinolones both provide greater in vitro effect, the clinical benefit over beta lactams is uncertain in patients with atypical pneumonias. No benefit of survival or clinical efficacy was shown to empirical atypical coverage in hospitalized patients with CAP.
Use supplemental oxygen, if hypoxia. Severe cases of IAEP may require noninvasive mechanical ventilation or intubation and mechanical ventilation.
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was successful in stabilizing one 40-year-old patient with AEP prior to diagnosis and treatment with corticosteroids.
Bronchodilators may be used, but benefit is unclear.
The vast majority of patients with IAEP require hospitalization due to the acute onset of severe dyspnea and significant potential for respiratory failure.
Patients with ICEP are usually managed as outpatients but may require hospitalization for acute exacerbations or other cardiopulmonary illnesses.
IAEP and ICEP are associated with allergic diseases and referral to an allergist is appropriate upon diagnosis.
Because ICEP may result in severe, chronic pulmonary dysfunction, patients who are resistant to corticosteroids or who relapse warrant further evaluation by a pulmonologist.
For IAEP, if corticosteroids are started early, the prognosis is excellent. Most patients have a full recovery and do not relapse. B

In a 5-year case series of 338 patients, nearly all young, male smokers, with AEP treated at the Armed Forces Capital Hospital, 126 (37%) were initially admitted to the ICU and three patients underwent mechanical ventilation. Those with a high BAL/blood eosinophil score had favorable outcomes in terms of hypoxemia, hospital days, intensive care unit admission, oxygen supply days, and steroid treatment days.

Patients with ICEP frequently relapse and should be followed closely after diagnosis. B Authors of a case series of 36 patients with CEP treated with corticosteroids found that centrilobular opacities on high-resolution CT and higher serum surfactant protein-D levels (>135 ng/mL) at diagnosis were predictive for relapse.

In a case series of 73 patients diagnosed with CEP with a median follow-up period of 1,939 days, 27 patients had a relapse, 2 patients developed steroid-induced diabetes mellitus, 1 patient developed pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacteriosis and 5 patients died of unrelated causes.
Among patients with Churg-Strauss syndrome, cardiac involvement is a serious manifestation of the disease, accounting for approximately one-half of deaths from this disease.

Like adults, EP in children is rare in developed countries and can be acute or chronic, primary (e.g., idiopathic, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, HES) or secondary (e.g., parasitic infections, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, drug reactions). Treatment generally relies on corticosteroids with or without immunosuppressors.

cell.label: Diagnose eosinophilic pneumonia (EP): pulmonary infiltrates on CXR or chest CT, and evidence of peripheral eosinophilia and/or >25% eosinophils in BAL fluid. Rule out secondary causes of EP.
On current or recent medications known to cause EP?
Travel to endemic areas for parasites associated with EP?
History of long-standing asthma?
Does patient or family have a history of autoimmune disease (e.g., SLE, Sjogren's, rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, scleroderma)?
Is the patient currently diagnosed with a malignancy or does he or she have risk factors for malignancy or history of radiation therapy?
Does the patient have a history of exposure to infection (tuberculosis, viruses) or is immunocompromised?
CONSIDER IDIOPATHIC (PRIMARY) CAUSES. Are there systemic (extrapulmonary) symptoms?
Consider the following:
• Churg-Strauss—associated with a history of asthma. Neuropathy commonly present. Check for P-ANCA. Usually MPO positive. Tissue biopsy reveals eosinophilic granulomas.
• Wegener's—associated with history of chronic upper respiratory/sinus problems. Nephropathy often present. Check for C-ANCA. Usually PR3 positive. Tissue biopsy reveals granulomas (no eosinophils).

• HES—additional end-organ involvement, especially cardiac. May affect kidney, liver, joints, GI tract, and skin as well. Frequently associated with myeloproliferative disease. Usually not assocated with ANCA.
Consider IAEP OR ICEP.

• IAEP is acute in onset and presents with high fevers, hypoxemia, and chest pain. May present as ALI or ARDS. Associated with beginning tobacco smoking or increasing frequency. Also associated with environmental exposures.
• ICEP has an insidious onset, usually greater than 1 month. Rarely causes severe hypoxemia. Seen more frequently in patients with history of atopy.
Consider tuberculosis, brucella, coccidioides, and viral infections, including HIV.
Consider bronchogenic carcinoma, Hodgkin's disease and T-cell lymphoma.
Check for additional systemic symptoms consistent with these diseases.
If no significant extrapulmonary symptoms, consider allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Check for IgE to Aspergillus, highly elevated serum IgE, and central bronchiectasis on chest CT.
Check sputum, BAL fluid, and stool for ova and parasites.
STOP all potentially causative medications. If there are systemic symptoms as well as a rash, consider DRESS syndrome.

footnotes.footnote: ANCA denotes antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; BAL, bronchioalveolar lavage; DRESS, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; EP, eosinophilic pneumonia; HES, hypereosinophilic syndrome; HIV, human immunodeficiency virus; IAEP, idiopathic acute eosinophilic pneumonia; ICEP, idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PR3, proteinase 3; SLE, systemic lupus erythematosus.
